title: hesed
summary: Exodus 34, Psalm 103, and Micah 7 describe God’s steadfast love alongside compassion, forgiveness, and faithfulness. Exodus places this language in God’s self-proclamation after Israel’s breach; Psalm 103 praises compassion toward frail people; Micah 7 closes with confidence that God will pardon and remain faithful. Ephesians 2 and Titus 2 speak of related New Testament themes—mercy, grace, and new life—but they do not use the Hebrew term named here. These passages illuminate a theme across Scripture without making distinct words interchangeable.
historical_context: The references include a narrative setting after the golden calf, a psalm of praise, a prophetic closing, and two letters’ teaching about salvation and conduct. These textual contexts support the explanation; the source list does not support a comparative history of the term.
canonical_context: Exodus 34 and Micah 7 place divine steadfast love alongside forgiveness and faithfulness; Psalm 103 praises compassion toward human frailty. Ephesians 2 and Titus 2 describe grace and mercy in relation to new life and conduct. The later passages echo related themes, but should not be treated as direct occurrences of the Hebrew term.
literary_context: Exodus records a proclamation of God’s character, Psalm 103 is praise, and Micah 7 closes with a question and confession of hope. Ephesians 2 and Titus 2 are instructional arguments. Their forms show how steadfast love is confessed, celebrated, hoped for, and connected with changed life.
covenantal_significance: The Hebrew references connect steadfast love with God’s covenant faithfulness, forgiveness, and compassion. The New Testament passages describe God’s mercy and grace bringing life and shaping conduct. Together they show a canonical relationship between these themes while preserving the words and arguments of each passage.
canonical_role: This entry gathers Hebrew-scripture portrayals of steadfast love and New Testament passages about related mercy and grace. It helps readers follow the thematic connection without assuming a single term or definition underlies every reference.

interpretive_notes.note: Do not reduce hesed to a single English gloss.
Check the immediate context and genre before drawing theological conclusions.
